nodes.name: permuted data / sparsely permuted data
nodes.statement: In this paper, we consider the situation where the identifiers of the predictors (or equivalently those of the responses) are subject to an unknown permutation so that correspondence between $y_i$ and $\x_i$ may not be be taken for granted. We refer to this situation as ``permuted data'' respectively ``sparsely permuted data'' when the permutation only affects a small fraction of all response-predictor pairs.
nodes.statement_short: A dataset is ``permuted'' when predictor/response identifiers are scrambled by an unknown permutation, and ``sparsely permuted'' when only a small fraction of pairs is affected.
nodes.genus: the situation where the identifiers of the predictors (or equivalently those of the responses) are subject to an unknown permutation
differentia: correspondence between $y_i$ and $\x_i$ may not be be taken for granted
the permutation only affects a small fraction of all response-predictor pairs

nodes.name: record linkage (entity resolution)
nodes.statement: Record linkage, or entity resolution, is an essential task in data integration. The task is to identify which records in different datasets belong to the same entity. In this context, the term "entity" is to be understood in a broad sense, and may refer to customers, tax payers or patients, etc.
differentia: identify which records in different datasets belong to the same entity

nodes.name: probabilistic record linkage
nodes.statement: Generally, due to the lack of unique entity identifiers in data files, record matching is based on methods of \emph{probabilistic record linkage} \cite{Fellegi69} that score similarity between common quasi-identifiers.

nodes.name: number of mismatches / Hamming distance $d_H(\Pi^*,I_n)$
nodes.statement: Let us consider the number of mismatches which can be expressed as $d_H(\Pi^*,I_n)\coloneq|\{ i:\: \Pi_{ii}^*=0\}|$, the Hamming distance between $\Pi^*$ and the identity matrix $I_n$.
nodes.genus: the Hamming distance between $\Pi^*$ and the identity matrix $I_n$

nodes.name: $k$-sparse permutation
nodes.statement: A permutation respectively its matrix representation $\Pi$ is said to be $k$-sparse if $d_H(\Pi, I_n)\le k$.
nodes.genus: A permutation respectively its matrix representation $\Pi$

nodes.name: broken sample
nodes.statement: A broken sample is a sample of $(y_i, \x_i)$-pairs that up to some permutation of the $\{\x_i\}$ (or equivalently the $\{ y_i \}$) are generated from their joint distribution. In other words, each component of $(y_i, \x_i)$ is observed separately (as if it were generated from its marginal distribution), with possibly different orders for each component.
nodes.origin_citation: DeGroot, Feder & Goel 1971; DeGroot & Goel 1976, 1980; Wu 1998

nodes.name: constraint set $\mc{P}_{n,k}$
nodes.statement: For $0 \leq k \leq n$, let us introduce the shorthand \begin{equation*} \mc{P}_{n, k} = \{\Pi \in \mc{P}_n:\; d_H(\Pi,I_n)\le k \} \end{equation*} for the constraint set of $\Pi$ in problem \eqref{eq:lsq}.

nodes.name: Gaussian width
nodes.statement: Moreover, for a compact and symmetric\footnote{A set $S \subset \R^n$ is called symmetric if $x \in S$ implies that $-x \in S$.} set $K \subset \R^n$, its Gaussian width is defined by \begin{equation} w(K) = \E\nolimits_{g \sim N(0, I_n)}\left[\sup_{x \in K} |\scp{g}{x}| \right]. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.2 Least squares estimation of $\beta^*$ if $\Pi^*$ is $k$-sparse, $k \ll n$
nodes.statement_short: Gaussian width of a compact symmetric set $K$: the expected supremum over $K$ of $|\scp{g}{x}|$ for standard Gaussian $g$.

nodes.name: the set $\mc{T}$ of normalized permutation differences
nodes.statement: In our setting, we use the Gaussian width \eqref{eq:gaussianwidth} in conjunction with the set \begin{equation} \mc{T} = \bigcup_{\Pi \in \mc{P}_{n,k}} \left\{\text{range}(\Pi - \Pi^{*\T}) \right\} \cap \mathbb{S}^{n-1}, \end{equation} where we recall that $\Pi^{*\T} \in \mc{P}_{n,k}$ is the inverse of $\Pi^*$.

nodes.statement: Let $\nnorm{\cdot}_0$ denote the $\ell_0$-''norm'', i.e., the number of non-zero entries of a vector.

nodes.name: support $S^*$ of $\Pi^*$
nodes.statement: Under an additional condition on the SNR, we may deduce from that bound that $\wh{\Pi}$ identifies the ``support'' $S^* = \{i: \, \Pi_{ii}^* \neq 1\}$ of $\Pi^*$.

nodes.name: mismatch vector $f^*$
nodes.statement: Introducing $f^* = \Pi^* X \beta^* - X \beta^* = (\Pi^* - I_n) X \beta^*$, model \eqref{eq:lrwp} can be re-expressed as \begin{equation*} \y = X \beta^* + f^* + \eps. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Define $f^* = (\Pi^* - I_n) X \beta^*$, turning the permuted model into a linear model with an additive sparse corruption term.

nodes.name: cone $\mc{C}(J, \alpha)$
nodes.statement: For $J \in \mc{J}(s)$, and $\alpha \in [1,\infty)$, define \begin{equation} \mc{C}(J, \alpha) = \{v \in \R^p:\, \nnorm{v_{J^c}}_1 \leq \alpha \nnorm{v_J}_1 \}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: ($s$, $\delta$)-restricted isometry
nodes.statement_short: $A$ is an $(s,\delta)$-restricted isometry when its $s$-sparse extreme eigenvalues both lie within $\delta$ of $1$.

nodes.name: $(s, \alpha)$-restricted eigenvalue
nodes.statement: Let $A \in \R^{N \times p}$. We define the $(s, \alpha)$-\textbf{restricted eigenvalue} by \begin{equation} \phi(s, \alpha) = \min_{J \in \mc{J}(s)} \, \min_{v \in \mc{C}(J, \alpha) \setminus 0}\, \, \frac{\nnorm{A v}_2^2}{\nnorm{v_J}_2^2}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: index-subset family $\mc{J}(s)$
nodes.statement: For $1 \leq s \leq p$, let $\mc{J}(s)$ denote the set of all index subsets of $[p]$ of size $s$.
nodes.genus: set of all index subsets of $[p]$

nodes.name: sparsely permuted linear regression model
nodes.statement: If the number of such mismatches is known to be less than or equal to $k\le n$, then there is an unknown permutation $\varphi$ on $[n] \coloneq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ so that: $\varphi$ moves at most $k$ of the indices, and $(y_1,\x_{\varphi(1)}),\ldots,(y_n,\x_{\varphi(n)}) $ are independent realizations from the classical linear regression model \begin{equation} y=\x^\top\beta^* +\epsilon, \: \text{where $\epsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ and $\x\perp\!\!\!\perp\epsilon$.} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: At most $k$ indices are mismatched, and after undoing the unknown permutation $\varphi$ the pairs obey the classical Gaussian linear model.

nodes.name: Gaussian design (G)
nodes.statement: In the sequel, unless stated otherwise, we assume Gaussian design for the $\{ \x_i \}_{i = 1}^n$: \begin{equation*} (\text{\textbf{G}}): \qquad \x_i \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} N(0, I_d), \; \; i \in [n]. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Standing assumption (G): the predictors are i.i.d.~standard Gaussian vectors.

nodes.name: sparse permutation regime $k \ll n$
nodes.statement: As motivated in the introduction, we henceforth turn our attention to the case of $\Pi^*$ being $k$-sparse, with $k$ ``significantly smaller'' than $n$. The allowable range of $k$ is addressed in our analysis presented below.
nodes.section: 2.2 Least squares estimation of $\beta^*$ if $\Pi^*$ is $k$-sparse, $k \ll n$

nodes.name: classical linear regression model
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} y=\x^\top\beta^* +\epsilon, \: \text{where $\epsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ and $\x\perp\!\!\!\perp\epsilon$.} \end{equation}

nodes.name: linear regression with permuted data (matrix form)
nodes.statement: \begin{align} \begin{split} \y &=\Pi^*X\beta^* +\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\: \text{where $\y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)^\top$ and $\eps=(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_n)^\top$} \\ \Leftrightarrow \; \Pi^{*\T} \y &= X\beta^* + \Pi^{*\T} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}. \end{split} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Matrix form of the permuted model: $\y = \Pi^* X \beta^* + \eps$, equivalently $\Pi^{*\T}\y = X\beta^* + \Pi^{*\T}\eps$.

nodes.name: random matching model of Neter, Maynes and Ramanathan
nodes.statement: the model in \cite{Neter65} assumes that for $i=1,\ldots,n$, \begin{equation} y_i=\begin{cases} z_i&\text{with probability $q_{ii}$}\\ z_j&\text{with probability $q_{ij}, \; i \neq j$}. \end{cases} \end{equation}

nodes.name: El Nino linear regression model
nodes.statement: \begin{align} \begin{split} \texttt{air.temp} & = \beta_0 + \beta_{\texttt{zon}} \cdot \texttt{zon} + \beta_{\texttt{mer}} \cdot \texttt{mer} + \\ &\;\qquad + \beta_{\texttt{humidity}} \cdot \texttt{humidity} + \beta_{\texttt{s.s.temp}} \cdot \texttt{s.s.temp} + \epsilon. \end{split} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Air temperature regressed on zonal and meridional wind speed, humidity and sea-surface temperature.

nodes.name: estimation of $\Pi^*$ and $\beta^*$ from partially mismatched pairs
nodes.statement: The main question to be studied here is how the parameters $\Pi^*$ and $\beta^*$ can be accurately and efficiently estimated from the partially mismatched pairs $(y_i,\x_i)$. Efficiency here refers to computational complexity of the procedure that outputs the desired estimates.

nodes.name: constrained least squares problem for $(\Pi, \beta)$
nodes.statement: We can naturally estimate $\Pi^*$ and $\beta^*$ by a least-squares approach as: \begin{align} \begin{split} (\widehat{\Pi},\wh{\beta})=\argmin_{\Pi,\beta} \:& \: \|\Pi X\beta-\y\|_2^2\\ \text{subject to}\: &\: d_H(\Pi,I_n)\le k, \end{split} \end{align} where $\Pi$ and $\beta$ run over $\mathcal{P}_n$, the set of all permutation matrices in $\R^{n\times n}$, and $\R^d$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Joint least squares over permutations and coefficients, subject to a Hamming-ball ($k$-sparsity) constraint on the permutation.

nodes.name: least squares with range constraint on the mismatch vector
nodes.statement: This prompts the optimization problem \begin{align*} &\min_{\beta \in \R^d, f \in \R^n} \, \nnorm{\y - X \beta - f}_2^2 \\ &\text{subject to} \; f \in \bigcup_{\Pi \in \mc{P}_{n,k}} \text{range}(\Pi - I_n). \end{align*}

nodes.name: $\ell_0$-constrained relaxation
nodes.statement: A first relaxation is given by \begin{align} \begin{split} &\min_{\beta \in \R^d, f \in \R^n} \, \nnorm{\y - X \beta - f}_2^2 \\ &\text{subject to} \; \nnorm{f}_0 \leq k. \end{split} \end{align}

nodes.name: $\ell_1$-constrained convex relaxation
nodes.statement: Relaxation \eqref{eq:relax_1} is still not convex, but following the standard approach of replacing the $\ell_0$-norm by the $\ell_1$-norm, we end up with the convex optimization problem \begin{align} \begin{split} &\min_{\beta \in \R^d, f \in \R^n} \, \nnorm{\y - X \beta - f}_2^2 \\ &\text{subject to} \; \nnorm{f}_1 \leq b. \end{split} \end{align}

nodes.name: Lagrangian robust regression formulation
nodes.statement: Since it tends to be difficult to choose $b$ appropriately in practice, it is more convenient to work with the Lagrangian form of \eqref{eq:relax_1b}. After re-parameterizing $e = f / \sqrt{n}$\footnote{This reparameterization is merely for technical reasons} \begin{equation} \min_{\beta \in \R^d, e \in \R^n} \frac{1}{n}\nnorm{\y - X \beta - \sqrt{n} e}_2^2 + \lambda \nnorm{e}_1, \quad \lambda > 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Lagrangian ($\ell_1$-penalized) robust regression in $(\beta, e)$ with penalty $\lambda \nnorm{e}_1$.

nodes.name: least absolute deviation regression
nodes.statement: Formulation \eqref{eq:relax_2} is related to least absolute deviation regression \begin{equation} \min_{\beta \in \R^d} \nnorm{\y - X \beta}_1 \end{equation}

nodes.name: permutation estimation for $d = 1$
nodes.statement: When $d=1$, that is there is only one predictor in the regression model, $\wh{\Pi}$ is determined as a minimizer of the optimization problem \begin{equation} \max_{\Pi \in \mc{P}_{n}} \{\scp{\Pi X}{\y},\scp{\Pi X}{-\y} \} \qquad \text{subject to} \;\, d_H(\Pi, I_n) \leq k. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.4 Estimation of $\Pi^*$ given an estimator of $\beta^*$

nodes.name: least squares permutation estimation given $\beta^*$
nodes.statement: Note that when $\beta^*$ is known, computing the least squares estimator of $\Pi^*$ reduces to solving precisely one of the two optimization problem encountered in \eqref{eq:permutation_d1} for $d = 1$: \begin{equation} \max_{\Pi \in \mc{P}_{n}} \scp{\Pi X \beta^*}{\y} \qquad \text{subject to} \;\, d_H(\Pi, I_n) \leq k. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.4 Estimation of $\Pi^*$ given an estimator of $\beta^*$
nodes.statement_short: With $\beta^*$ known, estimating $\Pi^*$ becomes a single Hamming-constrained linear assignment problem.

nodes.name: Proposition 1 (negative result for unconstrained least squares)
nodes.statement: Let $\beta^* = 0$ and $\Pi^* = I_n$, i.e., $\mathbf{y} = \eps$ and consider the estimator \eqref{eq:lsq} with $k = n$. Then there exist constants $c,C > 0$ such that with probability at least $1 - C \exp(-c n)$ \begin{equation*} \nnorm{\wh{\beta}}_2^2 \geq \frac{n}{2n + d}\frac{\sigma^2}{32\pi^2}. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 2.1 Least squares estimation of $(\Pi^*, \beta^*)$ without additional constraints: a negative result
nodes.statement_short: With pure noise and no sparsity constraint, the least squares estimator has squared norm bounded away from $0$ with high probability -- it overfits.
conclusions: there exist constants $c,C > 0$ such that with probability at least $1 - C \exp(-c n)$ \begin{equation*} \nnorm{\wh{\beta}}_2^2 \geq \frac{n}{2n + d}\frac{\sigma^2}{32\pi^2}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Theorem 1 (error bound for $k$-sparse constrained least squares)
nodes.section: 2.2 Least squares estimation of $\beta^*$ if $\Pi^*$ is $k$-sparse, $k \ll n$
nodes.statement_short: Under a Gaussian-width condition and $n > 9 \vee 4d$, the $k$-sparse constrained least squares estimator satisfies an $\ell_2$-error bound with an oracle term plus an excess term of order $w(\mc{T})/\sqrt{n}$.
conclusions: with probability $\geq 1 - \frac{7}{2}\exp(-c_{\epss} n) - 2 \exp \left(-\frac{1}{2} (d \vee \log n) \right)$, \begin{equation} \nnorm{\wh{\beta} - \beta^*}_2 \leq \frac{\sigma}{1 - \sqrt{\frac{4 d \vee \log n}{n}}} \left(\sqrt{\frac{5 (d \vee \log n)}{n}} + \frac{2 (1 + \sqrt{2}) \epss^{-2} \{w(\mc{T}) \vee \log n\}}{\sqrt{n}} \right). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Corollary 1 (support recovery and refitting)
nodes.statement: For any $\delta \in (0,1)$, under the conditions of Theorem \ref{theo:constrained_permutation}, if it additionally holds that \begin{equation*} \text{\emph{SNR}} > \frac{2 (1 + \sqrt{2})^2 \epss^{-4}}{\delta^2}\,\cdot \frac{k^2 \{w(\mc{T}) \vee \log n\}^2}{n}, \qquad n-k \geq 9 \vee 4d, \end{equation*} the following events hold with probability at least $1 - \delta - 2\exp(-\frac{1}{2} (d \vee \log n))$: \begin{align*} \wh{S} \coloneq \{i:\;\wh{\Pi}_{ii} \neq 1 \} = S^*, \quad\qquad \nnorm{\wh{\wh{\beta}} - \beta^*}_2 \leq \frac{\sigma}{1 - \sqrt{\frac{4 d \vee \log n}{n - k}}} \sqrt{\frac{5 (d \vee \log n)}{n-k}}. \end{align*} where $\wh{\wh{\beta}}$ denotes the ordinary least squares estimator based on data $\{(y_i, \mathbf{x}_i): \; i \in [n] \setminus \wh{S} \}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Least squares estimation of $\beta^*$ if $\Pi^*$ is $k$-sparse, $k \ll n$
nodes.statement_short: Under an extra SNR condition, $\wh{\Pi}$ recovers the mismatch support exactly and refitting on the clean observations attains the oracle rate.
assumptions: For any $\delta \in (0,1)$, under the conditions of Theorem \ref{theo:constrained_permutation}
conclusions: the following events hold with probability at least $1 - \delta - 2\exp(-\frac{1}{2} (d \vee \log n))$: \begin{align*} \wh{S} \coloneq \{i:\;\wh{\Pi}_{ii} \neq 1 \} = S^*, \quad\qquad \nnorm{\wh{\wh{\beta}} - \beta^*}_2 \leq \frac{\sigma}{1 - \sqrt{\frac{4 d \vee \log n}{n - k}}} \sqrt{\frac{5 (d \vee \log n)}{n-k}}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Theorem 2 (error bound for the convex relaxation)
nodes.statement: Let $(\wt{\beta}, \wt{e})$ be a minimizer of \eqref{eq:relax_2} with $\lambda = 4 (1 + M) \sigma \sqrt{2 \log(n) / n}$ for some $M > 0$. There exist constants $c_1, c_2, \epss > 0$ so that if \begin{equation*} k \leq c_1 \frac{n-d}{\log(n/k)}, \end{equation*} the following holds with probability $\geq 1 - 2 \exp(-c_2 (n-d)) - 2n^{-M^2} - 2 \exp \left(-\frac{1}{2} (d \vee \log n) \right)$: \begin{equation} \nnorm{\wt{\beta} - \beta^*}_2 \leq \frac{\sigma}{1 - \sqrt{\frac{4 d \vee \log n}{n}}} \left(\sqrt{\frac{5 (d \vee \log n)}{n}} + 48 (1 + M) \frac{n}{n-d} \epss^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{2k \log n}{n}}\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The $\ell_1$-penalized (robust regression) estimator achieves an $\ell_2$-error bound essentially matching the computationally hard formulation, up to constants and a $\sqrt{k \log n / n}$ term.
assumptions: Let $(\wt{\beta}, \wt{e})$ be a minimizer of \eqref{eq:relax_2} with $\lambda = 4 (1 + M) \sigma \sqrt{2 \log(n) / n}$ for some $M > 0$
conclusions: the following holds with probability $\geq 1 - 2 \exp(-c_2 (n-d)) - 2n^{-M^2} - 2 \exp \left(-\frac{1}{2} (d \vee \log n) \right)$: \begin{equation} \nnorm{\wt{\beta} - \beta^*}_2 \leq \frac{\sigma}{1 - \sqrt{\frac{4 d \vee \log n}{n}}} \left(\sqrt{\frac{5 (d \vee \log n)}{n}} + 48 (1 + M) \frac{n}{n-d} \epss^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{2k \log n}{n}}\right). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Theorem 3 (SNR conditions for permutation recovery)
nodes.section: 2.4 Estimation of $\Pi^*$ given an estimator of $\beta^*$
nodes.statement_short: Sorting-based permutation recovery succeeds w.h.p. when the SNR exceeds roughly $n^4$, and fails with probability at least $.35$ when the SNR is below order $n^2$.
assumptions: Let $\delta, \Delta, \eta > 0$, and let $\wh{\theta}$ be an estimator s.t.~the event $\{\nnorm{X \wh{\theta} - X\beta^*}_{\infty} \leq \sigma \Delta \}$ holds with probability at least $1 - \eta$

nodes.name: Lemma 1 (decoupling of $\wh{\Pi}$ and $\wh{\beta}$)
nodes.statement: Consider optimization problem \eqref{eq:lsq}. Then, if $n \geq d$, with probability one \begin{equation} \wh{\Pi}^{\T} \in \argmin_{\Pi \in \mc{P}_{n,k}} \nnorm{\pre_X^{\perp} \Pi \mathbf{y}}_2^2, \qquad \wh{\beta} \in \left\{ \left(\frac{X^{\T} X}{n} \right)^{-1} \frac{X^{\T} \wh{\Pi}^{\T} \y}{n}, \; \, \wh{\Pi}^{\T} \in \argmin_{\Pi \in \mc{P}_{n,k}} \nnorm{\pre_X^{\perp} \Pi \mathbf{y}}_2^2 \right \}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The joint minimization splits: $\wh{\Pi}$ minimizes the residual of $\Pi\y$ off $\text{range}(X)$, and $\wh{\beta}$ is the OLS fit given $\wh{\Pi}$.

nodes.name: Lemma 2 (bound on $\nnorm{\wh{\Pi}^{\T} \y - \Pi^{*\T} \y}_2$)
nodes.statement: Under the conditions of Theorem \ref{theo:constrained_permutation}, the following holds with probability at least $1 - \frac{7}{2} \exp \left(-\frac{\psi(\epss, d/n) \nu_n^2}{8} \right) - \exp(-\{ w(\mc{T}) \vee \log n\})$, where $\psi(\epss, d/n)$ is defined in \eqref{eq:lowerbound} below. \begin{equation*} \nnorm{\wh{\Pi}^{\T} \y - \Pi^{*\T} \y}_2 \leq \frac{2 (1 + \sqrt{2})\sigma \epss^{-2} \{w(\mc{T}) \vee \log n\}}{\sqrt{n}}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: The estimated and true permutations move $\y$ by at most $O(\sigma \{w(\mc{T}) \vee \log n\}/\sqrt{n})$ in $\ell_2$.
conclusions: the following holds with probability at least $1 - \frac{7}{2} \exp \left(-\frac{\psi(\epss, d/n) \nu_n^2}{8} \right) - \exp(-\{ w(\mc{T}) \vee \log n\})$

nodes.name: Lemma 3 (control of $\sigma_{\min}(X/\sqrt{n})$ and $X^{\T}\eps$)
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma_{\min}(\cdot)$ denote the minimum singular value of a matrix. If $n \geq 9 \vee 4d$, it holds that \begin{align*} &\p \left( \left \{\sigma_{\min}(X / \sqrt{n}) < 1 - \sqrt{\frac{4 d \vee \log n}{n}} \right \} \cup \left\{ \norm{ \left(\frac{X^{\T} X}{n} \right)^{-1} \frac{X^{\T} \eps}{\sqrt{n}}}_2 \geq \sigma \frac{\sqrt{5 (d \vee \log n)} \}}{1 - \sqrt{\frac{4 d \vee \log n}{n}}} \right \} \right)\\ &\leq 2 \exp \left(-\frac{1}{2} (d \vee \log n) \right). \end{align*}

nodes.statement_short: Analogue of the decoupling lemma for the $\ell_1$-penalized problem: $\wt{e}$ solves a projected Lasso, and $\wt{\beta}$ is the OLS fit of $\y - \sqrt{n}\wt{e}$.

nodes.name: Lemma 7 (upper bound on the probability of $\mathcal{A}_{\gamma}$)
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma, \delta > 0$. Consider the event \begin{equation} \mathcal{A}_{\gamma}= \left\{\min_{i<j}(\x_i^\top\beta^*-\x_j^\top\beta^*)^2\le \gamma^2 \right\}. \end{equation} Then $\p\left( \mathcal{A}_{\gamma}\right)< \delta$ if \[ \nnorm{\beta^*}_2^2>\dfrac{n^2(n-1)^2}{4\delta^2\pi}\gamma^2. \]
nodes.statement_short: If $\nnorm{\beta^*}_2^2$ is large enough relative to $\gamma^2$, then no two fitted values are within $\gamma$ of each other, except with probability $<\delta$.

nodes.name: Lemma 8 (fixed-design condition for permutation recovery)
nodes.statement: Conditional on $X$, we have $\p \left(\widehat{\Pi}(\beta^*) \ne \Pi^*\mid X \right)<\delta$ if \begin{equation} \min_{i<j}\left(\x_i^\top\beta^*-\x_j^\top\beta^*\right)^2>4\sigma^2\log\dfrac{n(n-1)}{\delta}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Given the design, permutation recovery fails with probability $<\delta$ once the minimal gap between fitted values exceeds $4\sigma^2\log(n(n-1)/\delta)$.

nodes.name: Lemma 9 (lower bound on the probability of $\mathcal{A}_{\gamma}$)
nodes.statement: Consider the event $\mc{A}_{\gamma}$ in \eqref{eq:Agamma}. Then, for all $n \geq 5$, $\p\left( \mathcal{A}_{\gamma}\right)\ge 0.85$ if \begin{equation} \|\beta^*\|_2^2\le \dfrac{1}{25\pi}n^2\gamma^2. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: When $\nnorm{\beta^*}_2^2$ is small relative to $n^2\gamma^2$, two fitted values are within $\gamma$ with probability at least $.85$.

nodes.name: Concentration of Gaussian processes
nodes.statement: \emph{(\textbf{Concentration of Gaussian processes \cite{Boucheron2013}})} Let $K$ be a closed subset of the unit sphere in $\R^m$ with Gaussian width $w(K)$, and let $g \sim N(0, I_m)$. nodes.statement: \emph{(\textbf{Concentration of the norm of Gaussian random vectors \cite{Vershynin2010}})}\\ Let $g \sim N(0, I_n)$. Then for all $t > 0$, $\p(\nnorm{g}_2 \geq (1 + t) \sqrt{n}) \leq \exp(-t^2 n / 2)$.

nodes.name: Concentration of extreme singular values of Gaussian matrices
nodes.statement: \hspace*{-.7ex}\emph{(\textbf{Concentration of extreme singular values of Gaussian matrices \cite{Vershynin2010}})}\\ Let $X$ be an $n \times d$ Gaussian matrix with i.i.d.~$N(0,1)$-entries. Denote by $\sigma_{\min}(X)$ and $\sigma_{\max}(X)$ the minimum respectively maximum singular value of $X$. Then for any $t > 0$ \begin{equation*} \p(\sigma_{\min}(X) \geq \sqrt{n} - \sqrt{d} - t) \leq \exp(-t^2 / 2), \qquad \p(\sigma_{\max}(X) \geq \sqrt{n} + \sqrt{d} + t) \leq \exp(-t^2 / 2). \end{equation*}
assumptions: Let $X$ be an $n \times d$ Gaussian matrix with i.i.d.~$N(0,1)$-entries

nodes.statement: \emph{(\textbf{Concentration of quadratic forms \cite{Hsu2012}})}\\ Let $A$ be a an $m \times n$ matrix, $\Gamma = A^{\T} A$, and $g \sim N(0, I_n)$. Then for all $t > 0$ \begin{equation*} \p(\nnorm{A g}_2^2 > \tr(\Gamma) + 2 \sqrt{\tr(\Gamma^2) t} + 2 \nnorm{\Gamma}_2 t) \leq \exp(-t). \end{equation*}
assumptions: Let $A$ be a an $m \times n$ matrix, $\Gamma = A^{\T} A$, and $g \sim N(0, I_n)$

nodes.name: Maximal inequality for Gaussian random variables
nodes.statement: \emph{(\textbf{Maximal inequality for Gaussian random variables})}\\ Let $g_1, \ldots, g_n$ be zero-mean Gaussian random variables such that $\max_{1 \leq i \leq n} \E[g_i^2] \leq \sigma^2$. Then for all $M > 0$, $\p(\max_{1 \leq i \leq n} |g_i| > (1+M) \sigma \sqrt{2 \log n}) \leq 2n^{-M^2}$.
assumptions: Let $g_1, \ldots, g_n$ be zero-mean Gaussian random variables such that $\max_{1 \leq i \leq n} \E[g_i^2] \leq \sigma^2$

nodes.name: Small ball probability
nodes.statement: \emph{(\textbf{Small ball probability})}\\ Let $g \sim N(0,1)$. Then for all $t > 0$, $\p(|g| < t) \leq \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \, t < t$.

nodes.name: NP-hardness of the least squares permutation problem
nodes.statement: We note that \cite{Pananjady2016} have shown that unless $d=1$ the optimization problem \eqref{eq:lsq} is NP-hard for $k=n$. The same is true for any $k$ that is defined as a fraction of $n$.
conclusions: the optimization problem \eqref{eq:lsq} is NP-hard for $k=n$
The same is true for any $k$ that is defined as a fraction of $n$

nodes.name: bias of the ordinary least squares estimator under matching error
nodes.statement: They show that as a consequence of matching error, the ordinary least squares estimator $\wh{\beta}^{\text{ols}}$ is generally not an unbiased estimator of $\beta^*$.
assumptions: as a consequence of matching error
conclusions: the ordinary least squares estimator $\wh{\beta}^{\text{ols}}$ is generally not an unbiased estimator of $\beta^*$

nodes.name: almost sure convergence of $\wh{\beta}$ to a wrong limit for $d=1$
nodes.statement: A result of a similar flavor is shown in \cite{Abid2017}. For $d = 1$, they show that the estimator $\wh{\beta}$ converges almost surely to a limit different from $\beta^*$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$, and they derive an explicit expression for that limit.
nodes.section: 2.1 Least squares estimation of $(\Pi^*, \beta^*)$ without additional constraints: a negative result
conclusions: the estimator $\wh{\beta}$ converges almost surely to a limit different from $\beta^*$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$

nodes.name: Theorem 1 of Pananjady, Wainwright and Courtade (minimax lower bound)
nodes.statement: Theorem 1 in \cite{Pananjady2017} indicates that the answer is negative: they show that for any estimator $(\wt{\Pi}, \wt{\beta})$, one has \begin{equation*} \sup_{\Pi^* \in \mc{P}_n, \; \beta^* \in \R^d} \E\left[\textstyle\frac{1}{n} \nnorm{\wt{\Pi} X \wt{\beta} - \Pi^* X \beta^*}_2^2\right] \geq c \sigma^2. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 2.1 Least squares estimation of $(\Pi^*, \beta^*)$ without additional constraints: a negative result
nodes.statement_short: No estimator can drive the worst-case normalized prediction error below a constant multiple of $\sigma^2$ when $\Pi^*$ is unrestricted.

nodes.name: SNR lower bound of order $\Omega(d/\log\log n)$
nodes.statement: Along this direction, another negative result is shown in \cite{Hsu2017}. They demonstrate that a lower bound on the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) \begin{equation} \text{SNR} = \nnorm{\beta^*}_2^2 / \sigma^2 \end{equation} of the order $\Omega(d / \log \log n)$ is required for any estimator of $\beta^*$ to achieve a non-trivial expected relative estimation error\footnote{Non-trivial here refers to a relative estimation error of lower order than that of the estimator $\wh{\theta} \equiv 0$.}.
nodes.section: 2.1 Least squares estimation of $(\Pi^*, \beta^*)$ without additional constraints: a negative result
conclusions: of the order $\Omega(d / \log \log n)$ is required for any estimator of $\beta^*$ to achieve a non-trivial expected relative estimation error

nodes.name: SNR $> n^c$ suffices for permutation recovery by $\wh{\Pi}$
nodes.statement: As shown in \cite{Pananjady2016}, the condition $\text{SNR} > n^c$ for $c$ large enough is sufficient for the solution $\wh{\Pi}$ of \eqref{eq:lsq} to recover $\Pi^*$, in which case $\nnorm{\wh{\beta} - \beta^*}_2^2$ scales as $O(d/n)$ as in the usual regression setting in the absence of an unknown permutation.

assumptions: the condition $\text{SNR} > n^c$ for $c$ large enough
conclusions: sufficient for the solution $\wh{\Pi}$ of \eqref{eq:lsq} to recover $\Pi^*$

nodes.name: $\mc{T}$ is contained in an $\ell_0$-ball of radius $2k$
nodes.statement:
A simple observation is that for any $\Pi \in \mc{P}_{n,k}$ and any $v \in \R^n$, it holds that  egin{equation*} 
norm{\Pi v - \Pi^{*\T} v}_0 = 
norm{(\Pi - I_n) v - (\Pi^{*\T} - I_n) v}_0 \leq 
norm{(\Pi - I_n) v}_0 + 
norm{(\Pi^{*\T} - I_n) v}_0 \leq 2k. \end{equation*} As a result, $\mc{T} \subseteq B_0(2k; n) \cap \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$, where for $0 \leq r \leq n$, the set $B_0(r;n) = \{v \in \R^n: 
norm{v}_0 \leq r \}$ denotes the $\ell_0$-''ball" of radius $r$ in $\R^n$.

nodes.statement_short: Any two $k$-sparse permutations differ on at most $2k$ coordinates, so $\mc{T}$ sits inside the $2k$-sparse sphere.
conclusions:

norm{(\Pi - I_n) v - (\Pi^{*\T} - I_n) v}_0 \leq 
norm{(\Pi - I_n) v}_0 +  
norm{(\Pi^{*\T} - I_n) v}_0 \leq 2k.

nodes.name: Gaussian width bound for $\mc{T}$
nodes.statement: By well-known results (cf.~\cite{PlanVershynin2013a}, Lemma 2.3), we hence have that \begin{equation} w(\mc{T}) \leq w(B_0(2k;n) \cap \mathbb{S}^{n-1}) \leq 3.5 \sqrt{2k \log(en / 2k)}. \end{equation} Moreover, it is not hard to show that $w(\mc{T}) \geq w(B_0(n-k;k) \cap \mathbb{S}^{n-1})$, i.e., there is a lower bound on $w(\mc{T})$ of the same order.
nodes.section: 2.2 Least squares estimation of $\beta^*$ if $\Pi^*$ is $k$-sparse, $k \ll n$
nodes.statement_short: $w(\mc{T})$ is of order $\sqrt{k \log(n/k)}$, with matching upper and lower bounds.

nodes.name: extension to general covariance $\Sigma$
nodes.statement: Our results generalize to the case $ \x_i \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} N(0, \Sigma), \; i \in [n]$, for a symmetric positive definite matrix $\Sigma \in \R^{d \times d}$ in a straightforward manner by defining a new regression parameter $\Sigma^{1/2} \beta^*$. An estimator of that parameter (as discussed in the sequel) and an estimator of $\Sigma$ can then be combined to form an estimator of $\beta^*$. Note that estimation of $\Sigma$ is not affected by the presence of an unknown permutation.
nodes.statement_short: Results extend to non-isotropic Gaussian design by re-parameterizing with $\Sigma^{1/2}\beta^*$ and estimating $\Sigma$ separately.

nodes.name: equivalence of the Lagrangian formulation to Huber loss regression
nodes.statement: In fact, \eqref{eq:relax_2} is equivalent to employing Huber's loss \cite{Huber1964} instead of squared loss, cf.~\cite{She2012} and the references therein.

nodes.name: maximum inner product over permutations equals the sum of order statistics
nodes.statement: In fact, it easy to see that \begin{equation} \max_{\Pi \in \mc{P}_{n}} \scp{\Pi X}{\y} = \su X_{(i)} \y_{(i)}, \end{equation} where $X_{(i)}$ and $\y_{(i)}$ denote the $i$-th order statistic of $X$ and $\y$, respectively, $i \in [n]$. Hence, for $k = n$, problem \eqref{eq:permutation_d1} reduces to two vanilla sorting operations.

nodes.statement_short: The unconstrained maximum of $\scp{\Pi X}{\y}$ is attained by matching order statistics, so the $d=1$, $k=n$ problem is just two sorts.
conclusions: for $k = n$, problem \eqref{eq:permutation_d1} reduces to two vanilla sorting operations

nodes.name: reduction of robust regression to underdetermined sparse regression
nodes.statement: The robust regression formulation can be reduced to a specific sparse regression problem in an underdetermined setting with $n - d$ samples and $n$ parameters, one for each observation in a given sample that is affected by partial mismatches between the $\{\x_i\}_{i = 1}^n$ and the $\{ y_i\}_{i = 1}^n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the objective to maximizing $\nscp{\Pi\eps}{X_1}$, construct a sign-matching permutation $\Pi_{\pm}$ whose inner product concentrates around $n \cdot 2/\pi$, then divide by $\sigma_{\max}(X)$.

nodes.name: Reduce to an equivalent objective in $\beta$
nodes.statement: Consider the least squares problem \eqref{eq:lsq} with $\y = \eps$: \begin{equation*} \min_{\Pi, \beta} \nnorm{\eps - \Pi X \beta}_2^2. \end{equation*} Omitting the term not depending on $\beta$, an equivalent problem is given by \begin{equation*} \min_{\Pi, \beta} -2 \scp{\Pi \eps}{X \beta} + \nnorm{X \beta}_2^2. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Specialize the least squares problem to pure noise and drop the $\beta$-free term.

nodes.name: Re-parameterize $X\beta$ in polar form
nodes.statement: Re-parameterizing $X \beta = u \cdot r$, with $r \geq 0$ for $u \in \text{range}(X) \cap \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$, we obtain the optimization problem \begin{equation*} \min_{\Pi, u \in \text{range}(X) \cap \mathbb{S}^{n-1}, r \geq 0} -2 \scp{\Pi \eps}{u} r + r^2. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Write $X\beta = r u$ with $u$ a unit vector in $\text{range}(X)$.

nodes.name: Solve for the optimal radius and lower bound it
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\wh{r} = \nnorm{X\wh{\beta}}_2$ and lower bound it by restricting $u$ to the normalized first column of $X$.

nodes.name: Construct the sign-matching permutation $\Pi_{\pm}$
nodes.statement_short: Build an explicit feasible permutation that pairs positive noise entries with positive design entries and likewise for negatives.

nodes.name: Identify the distribution and expectation of the constructed inner product
nodes.statement: All terms inside the first two sums are i.i.d.~from the same distribution as $|g| |h|$, where $g$ and $h$ are independent $N(0,1)$-random variables, and accordingly the terms inside the last summand are i.i.d.~from the same distribution as $-|g||h|$. Conditional on $n_{\pm}$, hence $\nscp{\Pi_{\pm} \eps}{X_1}$ follows the same distribution as \begin{equation*} \sum_{i = 1}^{n - n_{\pm}} |g_i| |h_i| - \sum_{i=n - n_{\pm} + 1}^{n} |g_i| |h_i|, \end{equation*} where $\{ g_i \}_{i = 1}^n$ and $\{ h_i \}_{i = 1}^n$ are two independent sequences of $n$ i.i.d.~random variables from the $N(0,1)$-distribution. The expectation of the above expression (conditional on $n_{\pm}$) is given by \begin{equation*} (n - 2 n_{\pm}) \E[|g||h|] = (n - 2 n_{\pm}) \E[|g|]^2 = (n - 2 n_{\pm}) \frac{2}{\pi}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: The inner product distributes as a signed sum of $|g||h|$ terms with conditional mean $(n - 2n_{\pm}) \cdot 2/\pi$.

nodes.name: Apply a sub-exponential concentration inequality
nodes.statement: From Proposition 5.16 in \cite{Vershynin2010}, we have the following concentration inequality: \begin{equation*} \p \left(\left|\sum_{i = 1}^{n - n_{\pm}} (|g_i| |h_i| - \E[|g||h|]) - \sum_{i=n - n_{\pm} + 1}^{n} (|g_i| |h_i| - \E[|g||h|]) \right| \geq (n - 2 n_{\pm}) \frac{1}{\pi} \Big| n_{\pm} \right) \leq \exp(-n c). \end{equation*} Hence, conditional on $n_{\pm}$, with probability at least $1 - \exp(-nc)$, \begin{equation*} \sum_{i = 1}^{n - n_{\pm}} |g_i| |h_i| - \sum_{i=n - n_{\pm} + 1}^{n} |g_i| |h_i| \geq \frac{1}{\pi} (n - 2 n_{\pm}). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Concentration around the conditional mean gives a lower bound of $(n - 2n_{\pm})/\pi$ w.h.p.

nodes.name: Bound $n_{\pm}$ via Hoeffding's inequality
nodes.statement: Consider the definition of $n_+$ and $n_-$ Observe that $n_{\eps, +}$, $n_{X_1, +}$, $n_{\eps, -}$ and $n_{X_1, -}$ are each binomial random variables with $n$ trials and probability of success $1/2$. By repeated application of Hoeffding's inequality, we hence have \begin{equation*} \p(n_{+} \leq 3n/8) \leq 2\exp(-n/32), \quad \p(n_{-} \leq 3n/8) \leq 2 \exp(-n/32). \end{equation*} Conditional on the events $\{ n_{+} > 3n/8\}$ and $\{ n_{-} > 3n/8\}$, we have $n_{\pm} \leq 1/4$ and thus with probability at least $1 - C \exp(-nc)$ \begin{equation*} \sum_{i = 1}^{n - n_{\pm}} |g_i| |h_i| - \sum_{i=n - n_{\pm} + 1}^{n} |g_i| |h_i| \geq \frac{n}{2\pi} . \end{equation*} Accordingly, the same applies to the event $\{ \nscp{\Pi_{\pm} \eps}{X_1} > \frac{n}{2\pi} \}$.
nodes.statement_short: Sign counts are Binomial$(n,1/2)$, so $n_{\pm}$ is small w.h.p.~and the inner product exceeds $n/(2\pi)$.

nodes.name: Normalize by the extreme singular values and conclude
nodes.statement_short: Convert the bound on $\nnorm{X\wh{\beta}}_2$ into one on $\nnorm{\wh{\beta}}_2$ using $\sigma_{\max}(X) \leq \sqrt{2n}+\sqrt{d}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: We have \begin{align*} \min_{\Pi, \beta} \|\Pi X\beta-\y\|_2^2 &= \min_{\Pi, \beta} \|X\beta-\Pi \y\|_2^2 \\ &= \min_{\Pi, \beta} \left\{ \|\pr_X^{\perp} \Pi \y\|_2^2 + \|X\beta- \pr_X \Pi \y\|_2^2 \right\}. \end{align*} The second part can always be made equal to zero by choosing $\beta$ such that $X \beta = \pr_X \Pi \y$. It hence suffices to minimize the first part w.r.t.~$\Pi$ and to back-substitute the result into the second part. Under model (\text{\textbf{G}}), $X$ is non-singular with probability one as long as $n \geq d$ which yields the second expression in \eqref{eq:decomposition}.
nodes.statement_short: Pythagorean split of the objective into a component orthogonal to $\text{range}(X)$ and a component that can be zeroed by choosing $\beta$.

nodes.name: Split the objective by orthogonal projection
nodes.statement: We have \begin{align*} \min_{\Pi, \beta} \|\Pi X\beta-\y\|_2^2 &= \min_{\Pi, \beta} \|X\beta-\Pi \y\|_2^2 \\ &= \min_{\Pi, \beta} \left\{ \|\pr_X^{\perp} \Pi \y\|_2^2 + \|X\beta- \pr_X \Pi \y\|_2^2 \right\}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Decompose the residual into its components in $\text{range}(X)$ and its orthogonal complement.

nodes.name: Zero the in-range part and back-substitute
nodes.statement: The second part can always be made equal to zero by choosing $\beta$ such that $X \beta = \pr_X \Pi \y$. It hence suffices to minimize the first part w.r.t.~$\Pi$ and to back-substitute the result into the second part.
nodes.statement_short: Choosing $\beta$ so that $X\beta = \pr_X \Pi \y$ kills the second term, leaving a minimization in $\Pi$ alone.

nodes.name: Invoke non-singularity of $X$ under (G)
nodes.statement: Under model (\text{\textbf{G}}), $X$ is non-singular with probability one as long as $n \geq d$ which yields the second expression in \eqref{eq:decomposition}.
nodes.statement_short: Gaussian design makes $X$ non-singular a.s.~for $n \geq d$, giving the closed form for $\wh{\beta}$.

nodes.statement: It is clear that $\mathcal{A}_{\gamma}\subseteq\bigcup_{i<j}\left\{(\x_i^\top\beta^*-\x_j^\top\beta^*)^2\le \gamma^2 \right\}$. Using the fact that $\x_i^\top\beta^*-\x_j^\top\beta^*\sim N(0,2\|\beta^*\|_2^2)$, we have \begin{align*} \p\left(\mathcal{A}_{\gamma}\right)&\le\p\left(\bigcup_{i<j}\left\{-\dfrac{\gamma}{\sqrt{2}\|\beta^*\|_2}\le (\x_i -\x_j)^\top\dfrac{\beta^*}{\sqrt{2}\|\beta^*\|_2}\le \dfrac{\gamma}{\sqrt{2}\|\beta^*\|_2}\right\}\right) \\ &\le \sum_{i<j}\p\left( -\dfrac{\gamma}{\sqrt{2}\|\beta^*\|_2} \le g \leq \dfrac{\gamma}{\sqrt{2}\|\beta^*\|_2} \right), \quad g \sim N(0,1)\\ &\le\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} \dfrac{\gamma}{\|\beta^*\|_2\sqrt{\pi}} \quad \text{by Lemma \ref{lem:smallball} in Appendix \ref{app:aux}.} \end{align*} Thus, it suffices to require that $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} \dfrac{\gamma}{\|\beta^*\|_2\sqrt{\pi}}<\delta$. Resolving for $\nnorm{\beta^*}_2$, this condition becomes \[ \|\beta^*\|_2^2>\dfrac{n^2(n-1)^2}{4\delta^2\pi}\gamma^2. \]

nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we may assume that $\Pi^* = I_n$. By construction of $\widehat{\Pi}(\beta^*)$, it is clear that $\widehat{\Pi}(\beta^*) \ne \Pi^*$ whenever there exists $i\ne j$ such that $(y_i-y_j)(\x_i^\top\beta^*-\x_j^\top\beta^*)<0$, that is, the order between $\x_i^\top\beta^*$ and $\x_j^\top\beta^*$ is different than that of $y_i, y_j$.

nodes.name: Union bound conditional on the design
nodes.statement: First, conditioning on the random design matrix $X$, we have \begin{align*} \p(\wh{\Pi}(\beta^*)\ne \Pi^* \mid X)&=2\p\left(\bigcup_{i<j}\left\{y_i-y_j>0 \mid \x_i^\top\beta^*-\x_j^\top\beta^*<0\right\}\right)\\\ &\le 2 \sum_{i<j}\p\left(y_i-y_j>0 \mid \x_i^\top\beta^*-\x_j^\top\beta^*<0\right) \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Union bound over the $\binom{n}{2}$ possible inversions, conditionally on $X$.

nodes.name: Apply the Gaussian tail bound and conclude
nodes.statement: Since $y_i-y_j\mid \x_i^\top\beta^*-\x_j^\top\beta^*\sim N(\x_i^\top\beta^*-\x_j^\top\beta^*, 2\sigma^2)$, using the usual tail bound for the Gaussian distribution for each term in the above sum, we obtain \begin{align*} \p(\wh{\Pi}(\beta^*)\ne \Pi^* \mid X)&\le 2\sum_{i<j} \exp\left( -\dfrac{\left(\x_i^\top\beta^*-\x_j^\top\beta^*\right)^2}{4\sigma^2} \right)\\ &\le n(n-1)\exp\left( -\dfrac{\min_{i<j}\left(\x_i^\top\beta^*-\x_j^\top\beta^*\right)^2}{4\sigma^2} \right). \end{align*} Hence, for any $\delta>0$, $\p(\wh{\Pi}(\beta^*)\ne \Pi^* \mid X) <\delta$ if \begin{equation*} \min_{i<j}\left(\x_i^\top\beta^*-\x_j^\top\beta^*\right)^2>4\sigma^2\log\dfrac{n(n-1)}{\delta}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Gaussian tail bounds give an exponential bound in the minimal gap, yielding the stated sufficient condition.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3, part (a)
nodes.statement: Combining Lemmas \ref{lem:up} and \ref{lem:fixed}, part (a) in Theorem \ref{theo:permutationrecovery} follows immediately for $\wh{\Pi}(\beta^*)$ from the previous lemma by invoking Lemma \ref{lem:up} with $\gamma = 2 \sigma \sqrt{\log\frac{n(n-1)}{\delta}}$. We then have $\p(\wh{\Pi}(\beta^*)\ne \Pi^*)\le \p(\mathcal{A}_{\gamma})+\left(1-\p(\mathcal{A}_{\gamma})\right)\delta<2\delta$ under the conditions of the theorem. The general version of the theorem results from \begin{align*} \min_{i < j} |\x_i^{\T} \wh{\theta} - \x_j^{\T} \wh{\theta}| &\geq \min_{i < j} |\x_i^{\T} \beta^* - \x_j^{\T} \beta^*| - 2 \max_{1 \leq i \leq n} |\x_i^{\T} (\beta^* - \wh{\theta})| \\ &\geq \min_{i < j} |\x_i^{\T} \beta^* - \x_j^{\T} \beta^*| - 2 \sigma \Delta. \end{align*} conditional on the event $\{ \nnorm{X \beta^* - X \wh{\theta}}_{\infty} \leq \sigma \Delta \}$. The assertion follows from an application of Lemma \ref{lem:up} with $\gamma = 2 \sigma \left(\sqrt{\log\frac{n(n-1)}{\delta}} + \Delta \right)$.

nodes.statement_short: Lower bound the probability that a single fitted value falls in a small interval, then use a Binomial tail to get two collisions with probability $>.85$.

nodes.statement: \noindent Let $\mathcal{B}:=\left\{-\dfrac{\gamma}{\sqrt{2}}<\x^\top\beta^*<\dfrac{\gamma}{\sqrt{2}}\right\}$. For \textit{i.i.d.} observations $\x_1,\ldots,\x_n$, let \[ u:=\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}(\x_i\in \mathcal{B})\sim \text{binom}(n, p), \] with $p$ as defined in \eqref{eq:ap1}. The event $\mathcal{A}_{\gamma}$ in \eqref{eq:Agamma} occurs whenever at least two $\x_i, \x_j\in \mathcal{B}$, i.e., the event $\left\{u\ge 2\right\}\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{\gamma}$.

nodes.name: first synthetic data experiment
nodes.statement: Below, we present the results of two synthetic data experiments that are meant to serve as illustration of the developments in the previous section. In the first set of experiments, we generate $n = 200$ observations from model \eqref{eq:lrwp} under $(\textbf{G})$ with $d = 10$, $\sigma \in \{.01, .02, .05, .1, .2, .5, 1\}$, and $k/n \in \{.01, .02, .05, .1, .15, .2, \ldots, .5\}$, where the support of $\Pi^*$ is selected uniformly at random. The parameter $\beta^*$ is generated from the uniform distribution on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. For each pair $(\sigma, k/n)$, we conduct 100 independent replications. We compare the following estimators: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] The naive estimator (ordinary least squares estimator) of $\beta^*$ that ignores the fact that a fraction of the data is mismatched; this corresponds to the choice $k = 0$ in \eqref{eq:lsq}. \item[(ii)] The estimator $(\wt{\beta}, \wt{e})$ of $\S$\ref{subsec:convex_relaxation} with the choice $\lambda = 0.2 \sigma \sqrt{\log(n) / n}$. \item[(iii)] A thresholded version of the estimator in (ii) that discards those observations corresponds to the largest $k$ elements of $\{|\wt{e}_i|, \; i \in [n]\}$, and performs a least squares re-fit using the remaining $n-k$ observations. \end{itemize} The estimator $(\wt{\beta}, \wt{e})$ is computed in \texttt{CVX} \cite{cvx}.

nodes.name: discussion of the first simulation results
nodes.statement: Inspection of Figure \ref{fig:simulations_1} shows that the approach (ii) improves dramatically over the naive estimator (i) as long as the SNR is not too small (for $\sigma = 1$ and $\sigma = 0.5$, there is no longer a visible improvement). The results look promising in that the tolerable fraction of permuted observations can be as much as $0.5$ as long as the noise level is small; "tolerable" here refers to the fact that the estimation error increases gently with the fraction of permuted observations as opposed to (i) with a sharp increase in error as $k/n$ moves away from zero. nodes.statement: Figure \ref{fig:simulations_2} reveals that for $d = 1$, the estimator $\wh{\beta}$ performs substantially better than the convex formulation yielding $\wt{\beta}$. That starts changing for $\sigma = 0.2$, while for $\sigma = 0.5$, the adverse effect of an increase in $k/n$ becomes clearly visible.

nodes.name: results of the El Nino record linkage analysis
nodes.statement: The results of least squares regression indicate an excellent fit of this model with an R-squared of about $0.9$. With the goal to mimic the situation of data merging based on non-unique identifiers, the data set is divided into two data sets A and B, with A containing the response variable and B containing the predictors. The variables \texttt{latitude} and \texttt{longitude} are maintained in both data sets, and used as quasi-identifiers for record linkage of A and B with the \texttt{R} package \texttt{fastLink} \cite{fastlink}. Since (\texttt{latitude}, \texttt{longitude})-pairs are generally associated with multiple observations, the linkage process is not free of mismatches. The merged data set in turn follows the format depicted in Figure \ref{fig:permutationmodel} with a permutation affecting the correspondence between responses and predictors. As shown in Table \ref{tab:relax}, least squares regression with the thus merged data set leads to an increase of the residual sum of squares by $27\%$. In addition, the estimates of the regression parameters of the linear model \eqref{eq:elnino} change noticeably. As an alternative, we consider the approach \eqref{eq:relax_2} studied in detail herein, where the parameter $\lambda$ is chosen as $\lambda = 2 c \wh{\sigma} / \sqrt{n}$ with $c = 1.345$ and $\wh{\sigma}$ being a robust estimator of the residual standard error. More specifically, we use the function \texttt{rlm} (short for ``robust linear model fitting'') in the \texttt{R} package \texttt{MASS} \cite{MASS} with its default arguments which is in exact correspondence to the above choice of $\lambda$, as follows from the connection between linear regression with the Huber loss and formulation \eqref{eq:relax_2} (cf., e.g., Proposition 3.1 in \cite{She2012}). The figures in Table \ref{tab:relax} indicate that this approach provides some remedy relative to the naive use of the least squares estimator based on the merged data set. The estimates of the regression parameters from \eqref{eq:relax_2} reduce the gap to those obtained with the original data set by about a factor of one half in terms of $\ell_2$-distance. Moreover, approach \eqref{eq:relax_2} also yields a better fit in terms of the mean squared prediction error on a collection of twenty hold-out sets obtained from leaving out different random subsets of 10\% of the observations; in each of those twenty runs, the hold-in data set is split and subsequently re-linked in the same manner as described above. The reduction in excess risk (relative to the least squares estimator) achieved by \eqref{eq:relax_2} in comparison to the naive least squares solution is again a factor of roughly one half.
nodes.statement_short: Splitting and re-linking the El Nino data inflates the OLS residual sum of squares by 27%; the robust formulation halves both the parameter gap and the excess risk.

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Regression problems in which the correspondence between responses and predictors has been lost can be traced back to classical work in statistics and naturally arises in the context of record linkage. Despite its long history, the problem has seen revived interest lately and has been analyzed through the lens of modern non-asymptotic statistical theory. An additional layer of complexity to be dealt with is the computational hardness of (quadratic) assignment problems. In the present paper, both aspects are taken into account under the assumption of sparsely permuted data. One central insight of our work is that the availability of an accurate estimator of $\beta^*$ may be helpful in circumventing the computational barrier associated with permutation recovery. On the other hand, preliminary numerical results for $d = 1$ indicate a gap in statistical performance between a presumably hard formulation capturing precisely the notion of a sparse permutation and a computationally convenient relaxation that introduces a loss of information. This observation deserves further investigation.
nodes.statement_short: An accurate $\beta^*$-estimator circumvents the computational barrier of permutation recovery, but a statistical gap between the hard formulation and its relaxation remains.

nodes.statement: The connection to robust regression comes naturally as observations with mismatch between $\mathbf{x}$ and $y$ are likely to induce severe errors in model fitting beyond the usual noise, and hence take the role of outliers. nodes.name: the additional constraint $\su f_i = 1$ is omitted
nodes.statement: We note in passing that one could additionally impose the constraint $\su f_i = 1$. However, it turns out that its addition does not yield significant statistical benefits, and it is thus omitted.

nodes.name: the Hamming ball constraint buys computation, not statistics
nodes.statement: As already pointed out in \cite{Pananjady2016}, the Hamming ball constraint in \eqref{eq:lsq} does not substantially change the fundamental statistical limits of permutation recovery. However, that constraint does help in that it gives rise to a computationally efficient estimator of $\Pi^*$, whereas the statistical achievability result in \cite{Pananjady2016} is for the computationally hard estimator \eqref{eq:lsq}.

nodes.name: two-stage approach based on matching fitted values to responses
nodes.statement: We address this issue by adopting a two-stage approach that uses an accurate estimator $\wh{\theta}$ of $\beta^*$ to match the fitted values $\{ \x_i^{\T} \wh{\theta} \}_{i = 1}^n$ to the responses $\{ y_i \}_{i = 1}^n$. This reduces to simple sorting operations, thereby avoiding the computational challenges associated with problem \eqref{eq:lsq}.

nodes.name: integer programming makes the given-$\beta^*$ problem practical
nodes.statement: From a computational point of view, this already constitutes a simplification as \eqref{eq:permutation_givenbetastar} reduces to an integer linear program; while problems in this class are still NP-hard in general, problem \eqref{eq:permutation_givenbetastar} can be considered as much more benign than the original problem \eqref{eq:lsq} which belongs to the class of quadratic assignment problems notorious for their computational hardness. Due to recent advances in integer programming that have meanwhile been taken advantage of for a series of other statistical problems \cite{Bertsimas2013, Bertsimas2016}, it turns out that problem \eqref{eq:permutation_givenbetastar} is practically feasible at least for $n$ in the order of a few thousands.
